text: Business Rules are powerful enough that the same five mistakes show up again and again in real instances. This lesson walks through each one, and the real fix for every single one of them.

The classic bug is the infinite loop. A rule on Incident that, on update, calls current dot update to save the record again, with no condition excluding its own change. Each update it performs re-triggers the exact same rule, which updates again, until the platform's recursion limit kills the transaction with an error. The real fix: inside a before rule, you never need to call update at all — field changes are already included in the one save.

Second mistake: not checking current dot operation. A rule configured to run on insert, update, and delete all at once can't assume it's only ever handling one of those. Here, opened_at gets overwritten on every single update too, because there's no check confirming the operation is actually an insert.

Third: writing logic as an after rule when it belongs in before. If the rule only needs to modify the same record being saved, putting that logic after forces a second, unnecessary database write for every single save. Move the exact same logic into a before rule, drop the update call, and you get one write instead of two.

Fourth: skipping Filter Conditions, so the rule runs on every single change to that table, not just the ones it actually cares about — wasting server resources checking logic that was never relevant. And fifth, writing table-specific logic on a base table's rule without scoping it, so an Incident-only fix quietly breaks Problem or Change Request too.

Five patterns, five fixes, all real and all well documented. Next, in the lab, we'll apply everything from this chapter and write two complete, working Business Rules end to end on the Incident table.
